cards.title: What is pressure?
cards.idea: Pressure is the force pushing on a surface, spread over the area of that surface. A smaller area means the same force creates more pressure.

interaction.prompt: Think of pressing a thumbtack into wood with your thumb. Tap to see why the sharp point hurts more than the flat end.

cards.reveal: The sharp point has a tiny area, so your finger's force concentrates there, creating high pressure. The flat end spreads the same force over a larger area, creating low pressure.

cards.title: The pressure formula
cards.idea: Pressure equals force divided by area: P = F ÷ A. Measured in pascals (Pa) in SI units, or in N/m².

interaction.prompt: Tap the diagram to label force, area, and pressure in the formula.

cards.reveal: A labeled diagram showing: Force (in newtons) at the top, Area (in m²) at the bottom, and Pressure = Force ÷ Area (in Pa or N/m²) as the result.

cards.title: How area changes pressure
cards.idea: When you keep force constant but change the area, pressure changes inversely—smaller area means larger pressure.

interaction.prompt: Slide the area slider left and right. Watch how pressure changes when force stays at 100 N.

cards.reveal: A simulation showing: Force fixed at 100 N. As area decreases from 10 m² to 1 m², pressure increases from 10 Pa to 100 Pa. The graph shows the inverse relationship.

cards.title: Pressure in everyday life
cards.idea: High pressure in small areas is why sharp objects pierce easily, and why we spread weight over larger areas to reduce pressure on soft ground.

interaction.prompt: Tap each image to see the pressure at work.

cards.reveal: Three labeled examples: (1) A needle point on skin—tiny area, high pressure, pierces easily. (2) A camel's wide feet on sand—large area, low pressure, doesn't sink. (3) A knife blade cutting—concentrated force on thin edge creates high pressure.

cards.title: Pressure in liquids and gases
cards.idea: Fluids (liquids and gases) exert pressure in all directions equally. Deeper in a liquid, pressure increases because more weight pushes down from above.

interaction.prompt: Imagine a diver going deeper underwater. Tap to see how pressure changes.

cards.reveal: At the surface, water pressure is low. As the diver goes deeper, more water sits above them, so pressure increases. Pressure acts equally in all directions—up, down, and sideways.

cards.title: Atmospheric pressure
cards.idea: The air around us has weight and exerts pressure on everything—about 101,325 Pa at sea level. We don't feel it because pressure acts equally in all directions.

interaction.prompt: Tap to discover why you don't feel the weight of the air above you.

cards.reveal: Atmospheric pressure pushes down on your head, but it also pushes up from below with equal force. These forces balance, so you feel no net pressure. This is why a barometer can measure air pressure—it shows how high air pressure can push a column of mercury.

workbook.prompt: A 500 N force is applied to two different surfaces: one with area 10 m² and one with area 2 m². Which surface experiences greater pressure?
Pressure is calculated using the formula P = F ÷ A, where F is force in newtons and A is ________ in square meters.
Why does a camel not sink into sand while a person in the same spot might?
options: Camels have wider feet that spread their weight over a larger area, reducing pressure on the sand
Sand under camels is harder than sand under people
Camels have special oils on their feet that prevent sinking
workbook.answer: Camels have wider feet that spread their weight over a larger area, reducing pressure on the sand

boss.prompt: A hydraulic press applies a force of 2000 N over an area of 0.5 m². A second press applies 3000 N over an area of 1.5 m². Which press creates greater pressure?
options: Cannot be determined without knowing the fluid type

boss.prompt: A scuba diver experiences a pressure of 250,000 Pa underwater. If atmospheric pressure at sea level is 101,325 Pa, the gauge pressure (pressure above atmospheric) is approximately ________ Pa.

A rectangular block of wood (mass 10 kg) can be placed on a table in two ways: flat side down (area 0.5 m²) or on its edge (area 0.1 m²). If g = 10 m/s², how many times greater is the pressure when the block stands on its edge compared to lying flat?
